3	# The foundations of the revival: the judgement
4	
5	## 0. How to read this
6	
7	- **The three layers**, his frame of 2026-10-26 05:25 UTC. L1, the language: the Working Draft (WD, the team's text of 2010-12, copied 2011-02-02), the revised specification, the papers of 2011, 2012 and 2019, the 2012 restart's Types chapter, the team's library as a statement of the language, and the team's later published word. L2, the team's implementation on the JVM: the compiled path's checker, code generator, class loader and run time, the compiler's prelude, and walk. L3, Java interoperability: how Fortress types and natives meet Java's. A ground in one layer does not by itself decide a question in another. Where a team text in L1 itself argues from L2 or L3 (as the 2011 paper argues from Java), the text is the team's L1 word and its argument is theirs to make; I count it as L1.
8	- **Verdicts.** *Holds*: the tenet is right and its sound reason exists in the right layer. *Holds, text*: right, but its entry states a weaker, misplaced or wrong reason, or lacks the reason the coordinator needs to weigh a trade-off. *Bends*: against a team text where the team left a way the revival did not take. *Reverse*. None of the nine is a bend or a reversal.
9	- **Consequential** is the coordinator skill's test: reverses, bends or reads anew a decision of his; touches microGPT; chooses where the three principles split or are silent; or cannot be undone. A ruling so marked is his; each carries a default.
10	- **Earlier judgements**: J0929 (`decisions-review/judgement.md`), R0929 (`popl-recheck.md`), J1023 (`type-decisions-review/judgement.md`), J1024 (`phase3-exit/judgement.md`). I do not repeat their rulings; section 6 lists where this review's evidence changes one.
11	
12	## 1. In short
13	
14	1. **His doubt is answered: no foundational decision was a mistake.** All nine tenets hold. Three were taken on incomplete or partly wrong information (P-42, P-43, P-37), and in each case the missing or corrected fact makes the decision stronger or leaves it unchanged. None weakens it.
15	2. **The layers were mixed in the record's reasons, not in his decisions.** Four entries state a reason in the wrong layer or with the wrong date: P-26's list of "later word" counts 2009 prelude code as later than 2010-2012 texts; P-43's "Why" calls the prelude "the team's last record of the Fortress way"; P-37 lets the one library "take a design of the prelude's" with no rule for when; P-42 says "the switch-over ends the departure" where one line of `Shell.java` does. One judgement of 2026-09-20 read a WD sentence (L1) as the reason to keep a compiled-path setting (L2); P-42 corrected the language rule nine days later, and the code change is still owed. The rewrites fix the reasons; no decision turns.
16	3. **The bound.** P-42 holds on L1 grounds now stronger than when he decided: POPL 2019 says `Any` in so many words; the WD's `Object` sentence is not in the 2008 text, enters in a 2009 bulk import, and the same WD section says type parameters take tuple and arrow types; the library instantiates at tuples; the 2012 Types chapter and Welterweight put tuples and `()` outside `Object`. Steele's 2012 commits implemented the WD's sentence on the compiled path ("amazingly, this was not yet implemented"), found it broke walk's tests, and confined it to the compiled path by a setting, inserting `extends Any` wherever the compiled libraries and tests needed tuples, arrows or `()`. That is enforcement of a written sentence on one path, not a choice of the language's rule; the team's later texts (Types 2012, POPL 2019) do not carry `Object`. The probe shows the compiled run time needs nothing for the switch: under `Any` tuple and arrow static arguments compile, load and run as they do with `extends Any` written; under `Object` the compile command silently miscompiles `id((3, 4))` as `id(3)` (row 691). Java interoperability points the same way: `java.lang.Object` is Fortress `Any` (`NamingCzar.java:447`). The bound is not a linchpin: only one line of `Shell.java` and ten test files rest on it.
17	4. **The prelude question.** A design of the compiler's prelude binds the one library when the team's later word on the language backs it, or when the team's text is silent or ambiguous and the team's own compiled checker enforces the design as a rule; a stub by the team's words, or an accommodation of a JVM or checker limit, does not bind; and "later" is a date, so a prelude line counts as later only if it is later than the library's text on the same shape and no later L1 text contradicts it. Under that rule the revival kept the interpreter library's text against a backed prelude design in exactly one place, row 816, reversed by P-158. The sweep's three dated designs do not bind: `fail(s: String): Zilch` (Steele 2011) is contradicted by the 2012 Types chapter and POPL 2019, which make `Bottom` inexpressible, and the revival's instance rule is POPL 2019's own; the order traits' `comprises T` (Steele 2012-06) spells a fact the checker now reads from the F-bound, and Naden's last word points to the bound-based form; `String`'s left-only concatenation has no team reason and the library's text and the specification's juxtaposition rule decide against it.
18	5. **Phase 3 closes with climb batch 22c**, which must carry four rungs: row 816's repair (P-158), row 782's nine operator headers with the export check reading operators (P-155 read to cover it), `List`'s two imports into the thirteen, and the bound `Any` for `fortress compile`. Its exit gate: the distance 0 over the thirteen, under the compile command's own setting, with operators and `abstract` read the team's way. Row 701, row 321, the 52 code-generator refusals and the natives are phase 4's. This moves the flip earlier than J1024 placed it.
19	6. **The rewrites** (section 5) are P-26, P-37, P-43, P-42, P-33, and smaller corrections to P-7, P-12, P-59, P-17/P-84, P-58. Each must make the coordinator weigh in the right layer, date "later" correctly, and know what the switch-over must run as well as check.
20	
21	## 2. The nine tenets
22	
23	### Tenet 1. The goal and its measure (P-7, P-8). Holds.
24	
25	- **Sound reason and layer.** The goal joins two layers on purpose: the intent is judged in L1 (the specification as the revival revises it, the 2012 Types chapter beside it); the measure is L2 (microGPT compiled to JVM bytecode, running fast). The language itself states the aim: the WD is "designed for producing robust high-performance software" (`philosophy.tex:14-18`, `:33-35`). P-8 is a rule of weighing, his words, and lists "the implementations" among the designers' sources: right, so long as an implementation's word is read as L2 evidence.
26	- **Where the entry crosses layers.** P-7's second sentence, "where the team's later work, in the compiler or in the papers on types, contradicts the original text, the text is updated to follow that work", is his 10-12 words and is the mechanism of P-26. "Later work in the compiler" is two things: a rule the team's checker enforces on purpose (L1 intent shown in L2 code) and an accommodation of the JVM or of a checker gap (L2 only). P-7 should not restate the rule; it should point to P-26, where the distinction lives (ruling 5).
27	- **Risk, not defect.** The team's wind-down named a conflict between the two halves (the type system against "a virtual machine not designed to support it"), and Steele's 2016 slide 45 proposed "a less complex type system". No measurement settles it for microGPT: no compiled kernel exists, no Java baseline is written. The tenet's two halves can pull apart at phase 5 and 6; that is the goal's own risk, known since 2026-09-08, and not a reason to change it.
28	- **Default:** stands. P-7's revision sentence points to P-26. Not consequential (a text edit the coordinator shows him).
29	
30	### Tenet 2. The team's later word wins (P-26). Holds, text.
31	
32	- **Sound reason, L1.** The WD contradicts itself (its types chapter: the numeric types "are mutually exclusive"; its library chapters: ℤ a subtype of ℚ) and was last edited 2010-12. The type group's texts of 2011 (OOPSLA), 2012 (Types chapter, Naden, Welterweight) and 2019 (POPL) are later and consistent on the exclusion rule, the three overloading rules and the default bound. Ranking later consistent texts above an earlier self-contradicting one is the right rule for this language, as J0929 F3 said.
33	- **Where the entry misstates.** (a) Its reason is an L2 motive: the type group "worked to make the language run, with performance as the goal and specialization a must, and learned what is feasible". A JVM limit the team hit is evidence about L2, not a reason to rank an L1 text. (b) Its list of the later word mixes layers and dates: "the number types of the compiler's prelude made siblings in 2009 and 2010" is L2 code, earlier than the WD's last edit (2010-12), earlier than the 2011 paper, with no stated reason (`6896886fb` is a code-generator commit whose message ends "this would be a good time to get coercion working"). (c) "Specialization kept" names an L1 thing in P-26 (an overload for one instantiation, chosen at run time) and an L2 thing in the skill's `exploring.md:20` (a class per instantiation). (d) "The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text" is the coordinator's sentence with no source (rq 215). (e) P-26 has been applied with L2 code as the later word in P-43's "Why", P-153 ("the team's later code") and P-158's reason. Of these, P-158 is sound for another reason (ruling 3); P-43's and P-153's conclusions are sound on L1 grounds the entries do not name.
34	- **The limit the exclusion brief named** stands: where two of the team's later sources conflict (the interpreter's nested library kept to 2012 against the prelude flat since 2009; the 2012 patents' forest rule against POPL 2019), P-26 gives no order, and P-8 decides by the goal. That is how route A was chosen and it is the right order of the two rules.
35	- **Default:** stands; rewritten to state the layer rule and the dating rule (section 5). Strike the "unfinished text" sentence (rq 215; nothing rests on it). Consequential in that it narrows what counts as "later word": his, and he said yes to the rewording on 10-26 07:42 UTC; the text passes the trap test before it enters.
36	
37	### Tenet 3. One library, the interpreter's (P-37). Holds, text.
38	
39	- **Sound reason, L1.** The specification knows one default library, "chiefly `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`" (`library/structure.tex:15-20`), and never names the compiler's. The interpreter's library is the team's statement of the language's library. The prelude is a bootstrap by the team's own words: "stripped-down minimalist ... first crack at compilation" (2008), "bogus" (2009), "bogo-trait" (2012), "Hopefully temporary hack" (`WellKnownNames.java:113-116`). The split's stated reason is L3, "importing java objects cleanly", and P-58 answers that reason. His goal of 10-26 ("avoid the need to port walk's library into the compiler's library; continue the type checker so that it accepts the fuller library") is the L1 reason and is not in the entry.
40	- **The premise, and what measured it.** The decision assumes the compiled path can run the library, not only check it. Measured: code generation per declaration refuses 52 declarations of the twelve that the checker passes (F-34); tuple and arrow static arguments run on the class loader, `()` dies (row 339), a generic dotted method with one tuple-typed parameter dies (new, no row). Not measured: any library jar loaded and run compiled. So the premise is unmeasured, not refuted. His own doubt of 2026-09-20 15:18 UTC ("it tells you nothing of how much work is to get the interpreter running with the compiler") was recorded as not answered; F-34 and J1024's two phase-4 zeros are now the answer, and the entry should carry it.
41	- **Where the entry crosses layers.** "The one library may take a design of the prelude's, as it took the prelude's flat shape of the number types": this reads an L2 bootstrap as a design source with no rule for when. The ruling he received on 09-20 called the prelude "a record of what they could do behind the JVM wall" (L2); P-43's "Why" calls the same prelude "the team's last record of the Fortress way" (L1). Ruling 3 gives the rule that resolves the two.
42	- **Default:** stands. The rewrite adds his reason of 10-26, states that the switch-over needs the library to compile and run as well as check (phase 4's second zero), and carries ruling 3's rule for prelude designs. His (he approved the rewording).
43	
44	### Tenet 4. The implicit bound `Any` (P-42). Holds, text. Ruling 4 gives the detail.
45	
46	- **Default:** stands, grounds restated; "functions" dropped (rq 218; the specification's own callout already says "tuples and `()`"); the flip of `Shell.java:372` lands in 22c. His entry; the flip is a code change the entry already promises.
47	
48	### Tenet 5. The exclusion rule and the flat number types (P-43). Holds, text.
49	
50	- **Sound reason, L1.** The exclusion rule is the type group's published position four times over: the 2011 paper (`exclusion.tick:141-152`), the 2012 Types chapter (`types.tick:355-376`), Naden's "blanket multiple instantiation exclusion for the semantic benefits and the simplicity of the restriction" (`justificationOfRTR.tex:496-497`), POPL 2019's [Anc-Same-Trait]. Under the rule a nested tower whose every level carries the self-typed algebra traits at its own type is impossible: one `ZZ32` would be `Equality` at five instantiations. The WD's own types chapter says the numeric types "are mutually exclusive; no value has more than one of them" (`types-vals-vars.tex:502`), kept word for word in 2012. Steele's 2016 talk draws the tower flat. Route C, the patents' forest rule, was built as a shadow and priced (F-46): its soundness rule is the revival's, not the team's, and it needs code-generator, walk and checker work the team never did. The 2011 paper's own argument for the rule cites Java ("it is already required in Java") and decidability; that is the team's L1 word making an L3 argument, and it is theirs to make.
51	- **L2 confirms, does not decide.** The checker's Return Type Rule relies on the rule (F-44, measured by `IncompatibleClassChangeError`); the team's JVM type mapping relies on it (`TypeMapping.tex:125`, Chase 2012, not cited by the exclusion notes); the prelude was flattened in 2009-2010 with no stated reason. These say the compiled path needs the rule; they do not say the language has it. The language's texts say that.
52	- **Where the entry misstates.** Its "Why" is L2→L1 and misdated: "the flattened prelude is the team's last record of the Fortress way" (2009 code, earlier than every text above; his phrase "the team's last record" was about the forest rule, rq 219), "and its route leads to the POPL 2019 paper" (the paper keeps the rule and has no numbers and no tower; he was told on 09-24 that "the fact underneath it is narrower than you read it"). "He cares that specialised code runs fast, not how a specialisation is chosen" joins the two meanings of specialisation and he said it was not an answer (rq 220). He was not shown the WD's "mutually exclusive" sentence when he chose (J0929 D4 found its absence from the brief), nor the right authors and dates (fixed 10-12). Both omissions understated the L1 case for the decision he took.
53	- **Default:** stands. The "Why" becomes the L1 grounds above, with the prelude's flat shape named as the team's compiled-world instance of the same answer and F-46 as the price of route C. The two sentences of rq 219 and 220 go to history. His (he held P-43 for his answer; one line to him).
54	
55	### Tenet 6. The phase order (P-33). Holds, text.
56	
57	- **Sound reason, L2 (a work plan).** The checker is the gate the compiled path runs first; code generation and the run time come after it; the natives are the switch-over's definition. The order was approved with phase 4 undesigned and its code-generation half unmeasured (W1 was launched after the yes). F-34 now measures that half at 52 walls.
58	- **Where the entry misstates.** "The interpreter's whole library" is wider than F-53's twelve, and his 10-26 goal says "the fuller library". No step names the bound flip (F-289). J1024 §6 already ruled the exit restated and two phase-4 zeros; I confirm. The 40 other components (F-290: 624 errors, 25 crashes) do not block the switch-over; they block P-12's step, so each reaches zero before that step or before the first program that needs it. That is the coordinator's view, his to confirm; it is sound.
59	- **Default:** phase 3 closes with 22c (ruling 5); P-33's phase 3 text restated as the thirteen under the compile command's own setting; phase 4 carries two zeros (the checker's and the code generator's over the thirteen); the 40 components placed before P-12's step. His (reads anew P-33's exit).
60	
61	### Tenet 7. Unboxed doubles and `double[]` arrays (P-17, P-84). Holds, text.
62	
63	- **Sound reason.** L1: the language's aim (`philosophy.tex`), value objects "an implementation may freely copy" (`objects.tex:38`), a `LinearSequence` of a value type "describes a sequence of 'unboxed' values" (`binary.tex:80`), Jan Maessen's note that the store under a sized array is what is unboxed (`future.tex:42`), the library's `nat` sizes on `Vector` and `Matrix`. L2: the code generator boxes every number (F-11); boxing is the main cost in Java models of microGPT's three kernels (row 306); the team's own direction is `Unbox.java` and the loader's empty "expando" stub. The entries cite the L2 measurement and the sizes; they do not cite `objects.tex:38` or `binary.tex:76-82`, which are the L1 grounds that answer "is unboxing the language's intent or only ours".
64	- **Where the record is inconsistent.** He was told on 09-19 that stamping "only renames", so no generic instance can hold a `double[]`; on 09-24 that "unboxing will build on" stamping. Both are L2 statements and both can be true (the class loader's way, A4, is unmeasured); the record must say so in one place. His 09-20 lean for the class-loader way was "recorded as your leans, to confirm" and is in no entry. Decision A (the mechanism under `double[]`) is the open risk of the "fast" half, as J0929 omission 3 said; nothing since measured it.
65	- **Default:** stands. Add the two L1 grounds; record his 09-20 lean under P-85 as a lean to confirm; state that stamping alone gives no `double[]` field and that A4 is unmeasured. Not consequential (text); the lean is his and goes to him as "to confirm".
66	
67	### Tenet 8. The natives' form (P-58). Holds; his informed yes owed.
68	
69	- **Sound reason, L3 with L1 practice.** The language has no foreign-function interface: the WD lists one among proposals (`future.tex:675`) and says nothing else. So the binding form is outside the language, an L3 choice, and the library's own practice decides it (P-27): every one of the 424 bindings is `builtinPrimitive("…")`. The team built both forms, `builtinPrimitive` for walk and `import java` for the compiler, and chose neither for the library. The entry's ground "the specification prints `builtinPrimitive`'s declaration" is weak: it is true only through the included library api, whose comment describes walk's mechanism. The sound ground is the layer and the practice.
70	- **What J1024 already ruled** stands: the yes must be informed and must come before climb batch 23, since after 449 bindings move the other form costs a library sweep.
71	- **Default:** stands as decided; his informed yes before batch 23. Consequential; his. The rewrite states the layer and the window in which the choice is cheap to undo.
72	
73	### Tenet 9. Walk runs the checker after the switch-over (P-12, P-59). Holds as a direction; its size is understated.
74	
75	- **Sound reason.** L1: Fortress is statically typed (`philosophy.tex:14`); coercion is resolved statically (`conversions-coercions.tex`). L2: walk has no static types; the checker inserts `CoercionInvocation` nodes. P-59 accepts walk's run-time choice as the interpreter's limit until then; R0929 §1.11 strengthened that reading (walk cannot implement the team's last dispatch model either).
76	- **Where the entry misstates.** "A small change of its own" (the coordinator's 09-29 words, not his) is wrong by reading: walk runs with Scala off and "The Java version of the type checker is gone now" (`StaticChecker.java:228-229`); walk has no case for `CoercionInvocation` (grep over `interpreter/` finds none); walk would then take the checker's own departures (rows 470, 731) as its own; and F-290's 624 errors stand between the checker and the components walk's programs import. P-59's "microGPT's static types are concrete" is the coordinator's premise, unmeasured (rq 221), measurable only when microGPT compiles.
77	- **Default:** P-12 stands as the direction; its text names the three pieces (the Scala checker on for walk, walk reading the inserted nodes, the components cleared) and says the size is unmeasured. P-59 stands; its premise sentence marked as the coordinator's, to be measured. Not consequential (direction unchanged).
78	
79	### Where the tenets' grounds pulled against each other, resolved
80	
81	- Tenet 3 against tenet 5 on what the prelude is: an L2 bootstrap; its shapes bind the one library only under ruling 3's rule. The flat numbers bind because the language's texts back them, not because the prelude has them.
82	- Tenet 2's "later" against tenet 5's dates: "later" is a date within L1; L2 code is not ranked by date against L1 texts.
83	- Tenet 5 against tenet 7 on stamping: both statements stand as L2 facts; A4 unmeasured.
84	- Tenet 3 against tenet 9: the twelve (thirteen) are the switch-over's; the 40 are P-12's.
85	- Tenet 4 against tenet 6: the flip lands in 22c.
86	- Tenet 6's "whole" against tenet 3's scope: restated as the thirteen; "the fuller library" is P-12's horizon.
87	
88	## 3. The prelude question: when a design of the compiler's prelude binds the one library
89	
90	**The coordinator's proposal:** when the team's later word on the language backs it, as the exclusion rule backs the flat number types; a bootstrap stub does not count.
91	
92	**Ruling: right, with three sharpenings.**
93	
94	1. **"Backs" is tested in L1 first.** A paper, the Types chapter, a specification sentence, a commit message or code comment that states the shape as the language's. The exclusion rule passes (four texts). The flat numbers pass through it and through the WD's "mutually exclusive".
95	2. **Where the L1 text is silent or ambiguous, the team's compiled checker enforcing the shape as a rule is the team's own reading of their text, and binds.** This is row 816's case: `apis.tex:252-256` reads as "no body needed" and is silent on the declaration; `source-code.tex:384-385` reads as the member declared either way; Chase's 2012 export checker counted every api member and refused a component that left one out. The run-time death (`invokeinterface` on the trait's interface) is the cost of the other reading, not the ground. So P-158 holds, and its stated reason should be this, not "by P-26, the compiled path's way wins over the interpreter's library" alone.
96	3. **"Later" is a date, and a stub is a stub by the team's words.** A prelude line counts as the team's later word only if it is later than the library's text on the same shape and no later L1 text contradicts it. A line the team called "for now", "bogus", "bogo", "hack", "temporary", or that works around a checker gap (static arguments written at every generic call, fixed arities in place of varargs), is an accommodation and does not bind.
97	
98	**Applied to the sweep.**
99	
100	- **Where the revival kept the library's text against a backed prelude design: one place, row 816.** Reversed by P-158. Nothing else in the sweep's 29 rows qualifies.
101	- **`fail(s: String): Zilch`** (Steele, `0886e9654`, 2011-06-13, replacing `fail[\T extends Any\](s: String): T` and adding a parser production). A deliberate design, and L1 in kind (a declared bottom result). It does not bind: the later L1 word contradicts it. The WD forbids writing `BottomType` (`types-vals-vars.tex:514-515`); the 2012 Types chapter makes `Bottom` uninhabited and inexpressible; POPL 2019 says `Bottom` "is intentionally not expressible in the surface syntax" (`ParkPOPL2019.txt:438`), and its [Solve-Step] binds an unfixed parameter to the intersection of its upper bounds and the expected type, never `Bottom`. The revival's way (the generic `fail` kept, the checker's instance rule P-48) is that rule. Walk cannot evaluate `Zilch` (`SkZilchLocal`, `InterpreterBug`). The record weighed the shape without the commit; the outcome is right. **Default:** keep; a FACTS line records the commit and why it does not bind. Not consequential.
102	- **`comprises T` on the order traits** (Steele, `655e65d53` 2012-06-05 adds it beside the F-bound; `59fdeff62` 2012-06-06 removes the F-bound). A deliberate design, L1 in kind (the self-type idiom; Naden: "The self-type idiom is realized with the comprises clause"). It does not bind the spelling: Steele's own message says the self type "may be an intersection of the declaring trait and the comprises clause", which is the fact P-146 gives `self` in bodies and P-157 in the exclusion test, read from the F-bound; Naden's last word, 2012-08-31, says the idiom "should be ... a separate construct which cannot be used as a first class type, but instead only in bounds" (`justificationOfRTR.tex:626-630`), the bound-based form; POPL 2019 has no self types. The prelude's spelling costs walk a stack overflow (row 407), the checker a stack overflow at eight clauses (route-c experiment §2b), and closes each trait to its parameter (`LexicographicOrder` had to take it too). The record's history of the idiom stops at 2011-12-06 and must be completed with the two commits. **Default:** keep the F-bound; a FACTS line records the two commits. Not consequential. (P-146's signature half and P-157's reasons were ruled in J1023 and J1024 and are not re-ruled here.)
103	- **`String`'s concatenation with `self` on the left only, right operand `Object`** (chf 2009; Steele widened the right operand 2011-10-12, "supports knapsack code"). A working shape with no recorded reason for the left-only restriction; no later L1 text backs it; the library's api had both sides for walk, and the specification's juxtaposition rule allows `1 || "a"`, which the tests assert. Measured compiled: the prelude's shape refuses `1 || "a"` (`SkCompiledLeft`). It does not bind. 109	## 4. The bound: P-42 holds, on these grounds
110	
111	**L1.** (a) POPL 2019, the type group's last published word, Steele and Ryu among the authors: "By default, each type parameter has an upper bound Any" (`ParkPOPL2019.txt:418-419`). (b) The WD's `Object` sentence (`trait-parameters.tex:49-50`) is absent from the 2008 release (page 67), enters the repository in two bulk imports of 2009-11, the first in a chapter headed "Not Yet Implemented Features"; its composer is not recoverable. The same WD section says "Type parameters are instantiated with types such as trait types, tuple types, and arrow types" (`:53-54`), and the WD puts tuples, arrows and `()` outside `Object` (`types-vals-vars.tex:136`, `:215-216`); so under the WD's own `Object` default no unbounded parameter could take what the WD says parameters take. (c) The library, the team's statement of the language's library, declares its element parameters unbounded and instantiates them at tuples (`Generator[\E\]`, `zip`'s `(E,F)`); only six functions write `extends Any`. (d) The 2012 Types chapter states no default and makes `Any` the top with `Object` excluding `Void` and every tuple type (`types.tick:232-238`); Welterweight and the 2011 paper have `Any` as the top. (e) The team's own 2008 commit left the bound "(either Object or Any)" open. Naden's August 2012 theory calls `Object` "the distinguished top type" in a calculus with no tuples or arrows, where the two names coincide; it is not a vote for `Object` over tuples.

113	**L2, the archaeology's finding and how to read it.** Steele implemented the WD's sentence on 2012-05-28 ("amazingly, this was not yet implemented"), inserting `extends Any` into the compiled libraries and nine tests wherever they instantiated at `()`, a tuple, an arrow or `Any`; commented it out on 05-29 "so that interpreter tests will pass"; and on 05-30 made it a setting, on in `useCompilerLibraries`, off in `useInterpreterLibraries`. The brief's phrase "Steele's 2012 code chose `Object` as the language's rule" reads too much into it. His message says he was implementing a sentence already written, not deciding one; when the sentence broke walk's tests he did not change walk or the library, he confined the sentence to the compiled path; and he had to write `Any` by hand everywhere the compiled world needed tuples. 171	
172	**What you asked.** On 26 October you wrote that you doubted whether the decisions the revival rests on were good and well informed, or a mistake. You named the bound as a possible linchpin, and you asked that the three layers be kept apart: what the Fortress language says; how the team built it on the Java virtual machine; and how Fortress meets Java.
173	
174	**The verdict, first.**
175	
176	- None of the nine foundational decisions was a mistake. All nine hold.
177	- Three of them were taken on information that was incomplete or partly wrong. In every case, the missing or corrected fact makes your decision stronger or leaves it as it is. None weakens it.
178	- The layers were mixed in the reasons written under your decisions, not in the decisions. Four entries give a reason from the wrong layer, or call a 2009 piece of code "later" than a 2011 paper. The rewrites fix the reasons. No decision turns.
179	
180	**The bound, in plain words.** A type parameter is a placeholder for a type, like the `T` in `List[\T\]`. Its bound is the largest type the placeholder may stand for. `Any` is the type of every value. `Object` is the type of every value except tuples (pairs such as `(3, 4)`), functions, and the empty value `()`. You decided that a placeholder with no written bound means `Any`.
181	
182	- The language, layer one, says `Any`. The team's last paper, from 2019, with Steele and Ryu among its authors, says in so many words that the default bound is `Any`. The team's library, which is their statement of the language's library, writes its placeholders without a bound and fills them with tuples. The 2011 draft's sentence saying `Object` is not in the 2008 text, appears in 2009 in a list of "Not Yet Implemented Features", and sits beside a sentence in the same section saying placeholders take tuple types, which `Object` would forbid.
183	- The team's build on the virtual machine, layer two, does not need `Object`. In May 2012 Steele implemented the draft's sentence on the compiled path, saying it was "amazingly" not yet implemented. The next day it broke the interpreter's tests. He did not change the interpreter or the library. He made the sentence a setting that is on for the compiled path and off for the interpreter, and he wrote `Any` by hand in every compiled library and test that needed tuples. That is enforcing a sentence on one path, not choosing the language's rule. No team text says the compiled path needs `Object`. A probe this week turned the setting off: tuples and functions as type arguments compile and run exactly as they do today when `Any` is written. With the setting on, as the compile command has it today, a call `id((3, 4))` compiles and silently runs `id(3)`.
184	- Java, layer three, maps its own `Object` type to Fortress `Any`, not to Fortress `Object`. Nothing in the record ever used Java as a reason for the bound.
185	- What you were told on 29 September had two errors: that "nothing in the code changes" (one line in `Shell.java` does), and that the 2012 Types chapter puts functions outside `Object` (it puts them inside; tuples stay outside). You were not told that Steele turned the setting on for the compiled path on purpose. Your yes rested on the tuples, and the tuples decide it. The decision stands.
186	- The bound is not a linchpin. Only one line of code and ten test files rest on it.

5What the revival changed in Fortress itself

299

Changes a programmer writing Fortress would notice, by area.

300

Numbers

301
    302
  • The number types are siblings under Number, not a tower, as the team's compiler library already had them. A wider type converts from a narrower one by a declared coerce.
    • 303
  • Fixed-width overflow raises IntegerOverflow under walk, as on the compiled path. To wrap on purpose, write ∔, ∸ or ⨰.
    • 304
  • An integer power answers its base's type. A negative exponent raises an error, except at the bases 1 and -1. For a fraction, write 2.0^(-1).
    • 305
  • SUM and PROD are generic. Under walk, a reduction whose element type nothing fixes runs. The checker still needs it written, also for BIG MAX and BIG MIN: SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#i] f(j).
    • 306
  • QQ is exact. A negative shift count shifts the other way. GCD and LCM are never negative. narrow keeps the low 32 bits. round sends an exact half to the even integer.
    • 307
  • The library's numeral type is IntLiteral, a sibling that the integer types, QQ and RR64 convert from. Walk's numerals are unchanged for now.
    • 308
309

Ranges. Ranges are over ZZ32 only. A range over ZZ64, NN32, NN64 or ZZ stops when built. A subscript of rank 2 or 3 is checked corner by corner, so a corner outside the bounds raises IndexOutOfBounds.

310

Arrays and the rest of the library

311
    312
  • fill takes a value; tabulate takes a function.
    • 313
  • The array types bound their elements: T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }.
    • 314
  • An array's index type is bounded by Index, which only ZZ32 of the integer types extends. Write I extends Index in your own generic over one.
    • 315
  • String's juxtaposition, and each of ||, |||, // and ///, is three top-level operators.
    • 316
  • On the checker, a list of RR64 or QQ has no <.
    • 317
  • Array storage is still boxed.

320

  • Walk converts by coercion at calls, bindings and assignments, picking the coercion from the run-time value.

  • Walk infers type arguments through coercions. A type parameter nothing fixes takes its bound, and one whose bound names itself stays open.
    • 323
  • Walk chooses between a generic and a plain declaration by declared types, not by order in the file.

  • At load, walk refuses some programs it used to run: an object extending two closed traits without being listed; two functional methods with no declaration on their meet; an object that leaves an inherited abstract method without a body, as five of the team's demos did before they were respelled; an override that overrides nothing.

6The original Fortress and the revival's resolutions

353

Custodians, not authors

354

The first principle of the protocol the work follows reads: "We are custodians of their language, not its authors." It asks the revival to finish what the designers intended, judged by the specification and by the library's own practice. Every agent is bound by the same rules through the skill it loads.

355
    356
  • No committed file claims credit for the revival.
    • 357
  • Where git doesn't record who wrote something, the authorship is rebuilt from the history. It's never guessed.
    • 358
  • Reasons go into commit messages and reports, not into the team's source comments.
    • 359

362

The team left three sources that disagree

363

The team left Fortress in three forms, with the type papers beside them:

364
    365
  • the specification, the text that says what Fortress is;
    • 366
  • the interpreter (walk) and its library;
    • 367
  • the compiler and its own, smaller library.
    • 368
369

These disagree in places. The revival changes the team's Fortress for one of two reasons only: two of these sources contradict each other, or a program fails. It reconciles them. Where the team's later work, in the compiler's library or the type papers, departs from the original specification, the revival follows the later work. It then updates the specification to match what it implements. A callout marks the passage, and Appendix I keeps the original text with the reason.

370

Example: the number types

371
    372
  • The team's interpreter library put the number types in a tower. A narrower type was a kind of the wider type: ZZ32 was a kind of ZZ64, and ZZ64 a kind of ZZ.
    • 373
  • The prelude went from siblings to a tower and back in 2009. Christine Flood declared its widths as sibling objects in March. Jan-Willem Maessen made them a tower later that month. David Chase cut the subtyping between the widths in August. Sukyoung Ryu added the first exclusion, ZZ32 excludes ZZ64, in October. Maessen and Eric Allen widened the exclusions and added the first coercions, from November 2009 to January 2010. Guy Steele built the comparisons and the integer operators on the flat prelude in 2011.
    • 374
  • In 2010 Justin Hilburn built the exclusion rule into the checker: no type may extend two instantiations of one generic trait. In the tower, ZZ32 is both an Integral of ZZ32 and, through ZZ64, an Integral of ZZ64, which the rule refuses. The siblings obey it.
    • 375
  • On 09-24 the curator chose to keep the rule. Batch 6 made the interpreter's library siblings too, on 09-27, so that the checker accepts it.
    • 376
377

So a model that remembers the tower remembers the team's interpreter library correctly. What it doesn't know is that the team's compiler had left the tower in 2009.

378

Left as the team had it

379
    380
  • Functional methods: a method with self among its parameters is called as f(x).
    • 381
  • Juxtaposition as an operator, and the whitespace rules. The grammar is unchanged.
    • 382
  • Declarations: x = e, var x: T = e, x := e.
    • 383
  • Loops and reductions are library code. A for loop, a comprehension and SUM turn into calls to library objects: a generator, which produces the values, and a reduction, which combines them.
    • 384
  • Evaluation is parallel by default. The revival pins the suites to four threads in the build file.
    • 385
  • Only the compiled path checks static types. Walk checks more when it loads a program, but these aren't static types.
    • 386
  • What the specification describes and the team never built is still unbuilt: dimensions and units, property declarations, regions, reduction variables, complex numbers.
    • 387

Where the revival resolved a contradiction

389

Dispatch on every argument

390
    391
  • Overloads that differ in static parameters. 392
      393
    • Original: one sentence of the Working Draft forbids this. The 1.0 release of March 2008 doesn't have it. In git, the sentence first appears in the specification's sources as Sukyoung Ryu re-imported them in November 2009. Neither implementation enforced it. The checker implements the type group's model of 2011, from their OOPSLA paper, which allows such overloads.
      • 394
    • Resolution: such overloads are allowed, and the specification states the 2011 model. The implementations and the library already overload across static parameters, and enforcing the sentence would refuse about 180 pairs of declarations in the library's apis.
      • 395
    • 396
  • The return-type rule. 397
      398
    • Original: the 2011 paper asks for the rule on every instance of a generic declaration. The checker tested one. A pair that broke the rule then passed the checker and failed the JVM's check of the bytecode.
      • 399
    • Resolution: the checker tests every instance, as the paper asks. Such a program now fails when it's compiled, not when it runs.
      • 400
    • 401
  • How walk chooses between a generic and a plain declaration. 402
      403
    • Original: the specification chooses by the declarations' types. Walk chose by their order in the file.
      • 404
    • Resolution: walk now chooses by the declared types, as the specification says. A program's answer no longer depends on the order of its declarations.
      • 405
    • 406
  • Generic declarations that exclude each other only as a whole. Both implementations refused such a pair. The 2011 paper accepts it, by reading the parameter types together. Both paths now follow the paper.
    • 407
  • Symbolic operators. The checker skipped their overloads. The team knew the gap: its appendix of proposed features calls the two subscript operators "not really a valid overloading". The checker now checks every operator.
    • 408

Traits and objects

410
    411
  • The exclusion rule. 412
      413
    • Original: the checker has enforced the rule since 2010, and the 2011 paper states it. The Working Draft doesn't, and some of its examples break it.
      • 414
    • Resolution: the specification states the rule. It keeps the examples that break it, marked "Not allowed". Without the rule, the checker's return-type rule lets through programs that die with IncompatibleClassChangeError.
      • 415
    • 416
  • What a comprises clause says. 417
      418
    • Original: four passages of the Working Draft read it as a statement about types, and so are false for some programs it allows. The Types chapter of the 2012 restart reads it as a statement about values.
      • 419
    • Resolution: every value of the closed trait is a value of a listed type. Read by values, the passages hold.
      • 420
    • 421
  • The vectors' algebra. The team's vectors are additive groups, and its library also adds an array and a number. By the team's rules these overloads are valid together, but the checker could not show it. The library stays as the team wrote it, and the checker now reads the self type.
    • 422

424
    425
  • The bound of a type parameter with no written bound. 426
      427
    • Original: the Working Draft says Object. The library uses its generic containers with tuples, which Object doesn't hold, and writes Any where it states a bound.
      • 428
    • Resolution: the bound is Any, because the library works only with Any.
      • 429
    • 430
  • A type parameter that nothing in a call fixes. 431
      432
    • Original: the implementations gave it the empty type Bottom, or left it unsolved, and some such compiled calls failed the JVM's check of the bytecode. The POPL 2019 paper of Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu gives such a parameter its bound, never Bottom.

    • Built: the specification states the paper's rule. The checker infers such a parameter at its bounds, never at Bottom. Walk gives it its declared bound, and leaves open one whose bound names itself, such as SUM's. Walk still gives Bottom in three narrow cases.

    • Not built yet: at run time both implementations still run a dispatched generic declaration at the value's type where nothing fixes the parameter. The compiled path waits for phase 5, when its dispatcher will carry the call's static return type.

    • 436
  • The index type of a subscript. The team wanted an index bounded by an Index type that excludes the ranges, but a[1, 2, 3] passes a tuple, and they needed "a magic to convert that tuple argument expression to something of type Index". The bound is built, and a tuple of Index types is an Index. That tuple rule departs from the team's text on tuples, and the specification says so.
    • 437
  • Sizes on the compiled path. The specification has size parameters. The compiled path couldn't carry them, but its code generator had a slot reserved for them. The revival fills the reserved slot, in the team's pattern for type arguments, and a program with sizes now compiles and runs.

Numbers

440
    441
  • Conversion in walk. The specification says that a call converts its arguments when that makes it apply. Walk had a note "TODO add checks for COERCE" at that place. Walk now converts the arguments, doing the work the team's note left to do.

  • SUM and PROD. SUM used catch-all operators on Number, which went with the tower. SUM and PROD are now one generic declaration each, over the element type's own algebra.

Fortress revival · foundations review · 2026-10-26

The foundations review, for you

The judgement's section for you, in plain words. It answers the doubt you wrote on 26 October. Each section ends with its references.

Six sections

  1. What you asked
  2. The verdict, first
  3. The bound, in plain words
  4. The compiler's small library, in plain words
  5. The decisions to take, each with a default
  6. Two things to know

1What you asked

On 26 October you wrote that you doubted whether the decisions the revival rests on were good and well informed, or a mistake.

You named the bound as a possible linchpin: one decision that much else rests on. The section on the bound says what the bound is.

You asked that three layers be kept apart. The team is Fortress's designers at Sun Labs.

  • Layer one: what the Fortress language says.
  • Layer two: how the team built it on the Java virtual machine.
  • Layer three: how Fortress meets Java.

2The verdict, first

  1. None of the nine foundational decisions was a mistake. All nine hold.
  2. Three of them were taken on information that was incomplete or partly wrong. In every case, the missing or corrected fact makes your decision stronger or leaves it as it is. None weakens it.
  3. Each of your decisions is an entry in the record of decisions, with its reason written under it. One of your decisions lets the team's later word win over its earlier text. The layers were mixed in the reasons, not in the decisions. Four entries give a reason from the wrong layer, or call a 2009 piece of code "later" than a 2011 paper. The rewrites, new texts for those reasons, fix them. No decision turns.
References
  • Point 1: judgement section 2, the nine tenets.
  • Point 2: the bound (P-42), the flat numbers (P-43) and one library (P-37); judgement section 1, item 1.
  • Point 3: the later word (P-26); the four entries, P-26, P-43, P-37 and P-42; judgement section 1, item 2.

3The bound, in plain words

A type parameter is a placeholder for a type, like the T in List[\T\]. Its bound is the largest type the placeholder may stand for. Any is the type of every value. Object is the type of every value except tuples (pairs such as (3, 4)), functions, and the empty value (). You decided that a placeholder with no written bound means Any.

  1. The language, layer one, says Any. The team's last paper, from 2019, with Guy Steele and Sukyoung Ryu among its authors, says in so many words that the default bound is Any. The team's library is their statement of the language's library. It writes its placeholders without a bound and fills them with tuples. The 2011 draft of the specification has a sentence that says Object. That sentence is not in the 2008 text. It appears in 2009, in a list of "Not Yet Implemented Features". It sits beside a sentence in the same section that says placeholders take tuple types, which Object would forbid.
  2. The team's build on the virtual machine, layer two, does not need Object. The team built two paths to run a program. The interpreter runs it directly. The compiled path compiles it to Java bytecode, then runs it. In May 2012 Steele implemented the draft's sentence on the compiled path, saying it was "amazingly" not yet implemented. The next day it broke the interpreter's tests. He did not change the interpreter or the library. He made the sentence a setting: on for the compiled path, off for the interpreter. And he wrote Any by hand in every compiled library and test that needed tuples. That is enforcing a sentence on one path, not choosing the language's rule. No team text says the compiled path needs Object.
  3. A probe this week turned the setting off. A probe is a small experiment that an agent runs. With the setting off, placeholders filled with tuples and functions compile and run exactly as they do today when Any is written. With the setting on, as the compile command fortress compile has it today, a call id((3, 4)) compiles and silently runs id(3).
  4. Java, layer three, maps its own Object type to Fortress Any, not to Fortress Object. Nothing in the record ever used Java as a reason for the bound.
  5. What you were told on 29 September had two errors. First, that "nothing in the code changes": one line in Shell.java does. Second, that the Types chapter the team wrote in 2012 puts functions outside Object: it puts them inside, and tuples stay outside. You were not told that Steele turned the setting on for the compiled path on purpose. Your yes rested on the tuples, and the tuples decide it. The decision stands.
  6. The bound is not a linchpin. Only one line of code and ten test files rest on it.
References
  • Point 1: the 2019 paper, research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019.txt lines 418 to 419; the draft's two sentences, Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/trait-parameters.tex lines 49 to 54; judgement section 4, "L1".
  • Point 2: judgement section 4, "L2, the archaeology's finding"; explorations/reviews/foundations/bound-archaeology.md.
  • Point 3: explorations/perf-probes/bound-any-compiled/REPORT.md; the silent miscompile, ledger row 691; judgement section 4, "L2, the probe".
  • Point 4: NamingCzar.java line 447; judgement section 4, "L3".
  • Point 5: Shell.java line 372; judgement section 4, "What he was told".
  • Point 6: the ten test edits, judgement section 4, "Defaults"; section 1, item 3.

4The compiler's small library, in plain words

The team built two libraries: the interpreter's full one, and a small one for the compiler. They called the small one "bogus", a "bogo-trait" and a "hopefully temporary hack". You decided that the full one is the one library, the only library the revival keeps. You asked whether we ported the small library's good designs back, or just taught the checker to accept whatever the full library said. The checker is the type checker: it checks a program's types before the program is compiled.

  1. Both happened. The sweep is a review of the designs where the two libraries differ. It finds that the choice was weighed every time the two differed on a design.
    • Taken from the small library:
      • the flat number types, side by side, where no number type is a kind of another;
      • the numeral type, the type of a whole number written in a program;
      • ranges over 32-bit integers;
      • each integer type's own MIN and MAX;
      • the integer power;
      • lazy comparison;
      • the abstract members. Each library part has an interface, which lists what the part provides, and a component, which provides it. The rule: a component declares every member that its interface marks abstract.
    • Weighed and not taken, with the reason now dated:
      • The small library's fail returning a declared bottom type (Steele, June 2011). fail raises an error with a message. The bottom type is the type with no values. The team's own 2012 and 2019 texts later made that type unwritable.
      • The small library's comprises T spelling of the self type (Steele, June 2012). The self type is a placeholder that stands for the type that implements it. The checker now reads that fact from the placeholder's bound, as the last note of Naden, of the team's type group, pointed.
      • String concatenation with the string on the left only. The specification's own rule contradicts it.
  2. The rule for the future goes into the record. A design of the small library binds the full one in two cases: when the team's later word on the language backs it; or when the team's text is unclear and the team's own checker enforced the design as a rule. A stub, a stand-in by the team's own words, does not bind. "Later" is a date: a 2009 line of code is not later than a 2011 paper.
  3. One place, the abstract members. There we had the full library's text against a design of the small one that this rule binds. You reversed that on 25 October. The sweep finds no other.
References
  • Opening: "Hopefully temporary hack", WellKnownNames.java lines 113 to 116; judgement section 2, tenet 3.
  • Point 1: the sweep, explorations/reviews/foundations/prelude-lens.md; fail, commit 0886e9654; comprises T, commits 655e65d53 and 59fdeff62; Naden's note, Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex lines 626 to 630; judgement section 3, "Applied to the sweep".
  • Point 2: judgement section 3, the ruling and its three sharpenings.
  • Point 3: ledger row 816; P-158.

5The decisions to take, each with a default

1. Close phase 3 with climb batch 22c

  • A climb batch is one run of the workflow in which agents build a set of rungs. A rung is one piece of work, checked before it lands. Climb batch 22c is a batch not yet run.
  • Phase 3 is the work that made the type checker accept the full library's twelve core parts without error. Your framing is sound.
  • The batch carries four rungs:
    1. the abstract-member repair you decided;
    2. the nine operator headers that differ between interface and component, with the export check made to read operators. The export check is the checker's test that each component provides what its interface lists;
    3. the two library parts that List imports, which the checker's error count never covered;
    4. the one line that gives the compile command the Any bound, with ten test edits.
  • The batch's exit: the checker reports no error over those thirteen parts, under the compile command's own setting. The thirteen parts are the twelve core parts with the parts that List imports.
  • Phase 4 is the next phase. It leads to the switch-over: the point where the compiled path moves onto the full library and the small library is deleted. Everything that is about generating or running code stays in phase 4.

Default: yes.

2. Confirm that the 40 other library parts do not block the switch-over

  • They hold 624 errors.
  • They block the later step where the interpreter runs the checker on its own programs.
  • Each is cleared before that step, or before the first program that needs it.

Default: yes.

3. Rewrite the reasons under five entries, through the trap test you approved

  • The entries: the team's later word, one library, the flat numbers, the bound, and the phases. Smaller corrections go to five more.
  • The new texts must make the coordinator weigh in the right layer and date "later" correctly. The coordinator is the session that plans the work and runs the agents.
  • The trap test sets a case built to mislead, and checks that the new text leads the coordinator to the right choice.
  • You said yes to this on 26 October.

Default: proceed. Nothing enters until a trap test passes.

4. Three one-word answers, each in your own entry

  • Drop "functions" from the bound's entry, since the team's texts disagree on functions and agree on tuples. Default: drop.
  • Strike this sentence from the later-word entry: "The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text". The coordinator added it with no source. Default: strike.
  • Each entry gives its reason under the heading "Why". Move the two sentences of the flat-numbers entry's "Why" to history, and write the language's grounds in their place. Default: yes.

5. Say yes, informed, to the natives' form before batch 23

  • A native is a library function whose body is Java.
  • The decision keeps the library's own form, builtinPrimitive("..."), and changes only the string, to name a static Java method that both paths can call.
  • The language has no rule here, so the library's practice decides.
  • Batch 23 is phase 4's first batch. After the 449 bindings move, the other form, the compiler's import java, costs a library sweep: a pass over the whole library.

Default: yes, as decided.

6. One lean to confirm, no decision yet

  • On 20 September you leaned to the class loader as the way to store a vector of doubles as a Java double[]. The class loader is the part of the compiled path that makes Java classes while a program runs.
  • The lean was never recorded.
  • Record it as a lean under the array decisions, to be measured.
  • Today the loader stamps out a class per type. Stamping alone gives no double[] field.

Default: record as a lean.

References
  • Point 1: the abstract-member repair, row 816 and P-158; the operator headers, row 782 and P-155; List's imports, CovariantCollection and OneShotFlag; the line, Shell.java line 372; judgement section 5.
  • Point 2: the 40 parts and their 624 errors, F-290; the later step, P-12; judgement section 2, tenet 6.
  • Point 3: the five entries, P-26, P-37, P-43, P-42 and P-33; the five more, P-7, P-12, P-59, P-17 with P-84, and P-58, judgement section 1, item 6; what each new text must make the coordinator do, judgement section 7.
  • Point 4: the bound, P-42, review queue item 218; the later word, P-26, item 215; the flat numbers, P-43, items 219 and 220.
  • Point 5: P-58; judgement section 2, tenet 8.
  • Point 6: the array decisions, P-85; judgement section 2, tenet 7.

6Two things to know

No decision needed.

  1. A defect that does not depend on the bound. The probe found it on the compiled path: a generic method with one tuple-typed parameter dies at the call. It gets a row in the gap ledger, the file with one numbered row for each known gap or defect.
  2. Two kinds of cast failure. The small library's cast failure is an unchecked exception, where the full library's is checked. A function must name a checked exception in its throws clause; it need not name an unchecked one. This matters only when the checker starts checking throws clauses, and it will come to you then.
References
  • Point 1: CodeGen.java lines 6250 to 6263; judgement section 4, "L2, the probe".
  • Point 2: the small library's CastException and the full library's CastError; the throws check, row 352; judgement section 3, the two side findings.

From section 9 of explorations/reviews/foundations/judgement.md, the foundations review's judgement, written 2026-10-26 and committed as b007f65ff. "Judgement section" in the references means a section of that file.

3The bound, in plain words
A type parameter is a placeholder for a type, like the T in List[\T\]. Its bound is the largest type the placeholder may stand for. Any is the type of every value. Object is the type of every value except tuples (pairs such as (3, 4)), functions, and the empty value (). You decided that a placeholder with no written bound means Any.
The language, layer one, says Any. The team's last paper, from 2019, with Guy Steele and Sukyoung Ryu among its authors, says in so many words that the default bound is Any. The team's library is their statement of the language's library. It writes its placeholders without a bound and fills them with tuples. The 2011 draft of the specification has a sentence that says Object. That sentence is not in the 2008 text. It appears in 2009, in a list of "Not Yet Implemented Features". It sits beside a sentence in the same section that says placeholders take tuple types, which Object would forbid.
The team's build on the virtual machine, layer two, does not need Object. The team built two paths to run a program. The interpreter runs it directly. The compiled path compiles it to Java bytecode, then runs it. In May 2012 Steele implemented the draft's sentence on the compiled path, saying it was "amazingly" not yet implemented. The next day it broke the interpreter's tests. He did not change the interpreter or the library. He made the sentence a setting: on for the compiled path, off for the interpreter. And he wrote Any by hand in every compiled library and test that needed tuples. That is enforcing a sentence on one path, not choosing the language's rule. No team text says the compiled path needs Object.
A probe this week turned the setting off. A probe is a small experiment that an agent runs. With the setting off, placeholders filled with tuples and functions compile and run exactly as they do today when Any is written. With the setting on, as the compile command fortress compile has it today, a call id((3, 4)) compiles and silently runs id(3).
Java, layer three, maps its own Object type to Fortress Any, not to Fortress Object. Nothing in the record ever used Java as a reason for the bound.

The bound is not a linchpin. Only one line of code and ten test files rest on it.
